subject: MGMT363
title: Cognitive Bias, Uncertainty and Better Decisions

questions.stem: Describe confirmation bias.
options: Seeking evidence that supports what you already think
The first number dragging later estimates
What comes to mind easily feeling more likely
Past spending used as a reason to keep spending
questions.why: The survey designed to prove the manager right. See §6.1.

questions.stem: Describe anchoring.
options: The first number heard drags every later estimate toward it
The wish for agreement suppressing objection
questions.why: The supplier names a price and all bargaining orbits it. See §6.1.

questions.stem: Describe availability bias.
options: What comes to mind easily feels more likely than it is
The first number anchors later ones
questions.why: One vivid complaint outweighs a year of quiet data. See §6.1.

questions.stem: Describe sunk cost.
options: Past spending treated as a reason to keep spending
questions.why: 'We have put two years into this system already.' See §6.1.

questions.stem: Describe overconfidence.
options: Confidence in a forecast exceeds its accuracy
Treating past spending as a reason
questions.why: The launch date nobody has ever met is set again. See §6.1.

questions.stem: Describe groupthink.
options: The wish for agreement suppresses the objection — everyone nods, three disagree privately
The first number anchors the rest
questions.why: Everyone nods; three people privately disagree. See §6.1.

questions.stem: Identify the number of examinable biases in the chapter.
questions.why: Six used accurately beats twenty recognised vaguely. See §6.1.

questions.stem: Explain the uncomfortable finding about bias awareness.
options: Knowing about a bias does not protect you from it in the moment
questions.why: People just taught anchoring still anchor. See §6.2.

questions.stem: Describe what awareness does give you.
options: The ability to recognise the pattern in others' reasoning, and afterwards in your own
questions.why: Useful for diagnosis, which CLO 2 assesses. See §6.2.

questions.stem: Explain what follows from 'knowing does not remove it'.
options: Debiasing must be built into the process, not left to individual vigilance
questions.why: Design the meeting so the bias cannot operate. See §6.2.

questions.stem: Explain the argument for method that §6.2 gives.
options: Tools exist because unaided judgement is predictably wrong in known directions
questions.why: Not because the tools are clever. See §6.2.

questions.stem: Identify the set reading that supports §6.2.
questions.why: Kahneman (2011) is set reading. See §6.2.

questions.stem: Describe risk.
options: You know the possible outcomes and roughly their odds — like a machine failure rate from ten years of logs
You know neither the odds nor all the outcomes
questions.why: Risk: calculate. See §6.3.

questions.stem: Describe uncertainty.
options: You know neither the odds nor all the outcomes — like how customers will react to a new format
questions.why: Uncertainty: test cheaply. See §6.3.

questions.stem: Identify the right move under risk.
questions.why: Risk is calculable. See §6.3.

questions.stem: Identify the right move under uncertainty.
options: Build a spreadsheet of invented probabilities
questions.why: Chapter 8 takes the second column. See §6.3.

questions.stem: Explain the error that costs most.
options: Dressing uncertainty up as risk — a five-year forecast with two decimal places
questions.why: Overconfidence with formatting. See §6.3.

questions.stem: Describe 'write before you speak'.
options: Everyone records a view privately before discussion opens
One person argues against the answer
questions.why: Attacks groupthink and anchoring. See §6.4.

questions.stem: Describe 'assign a challenger'.
options: One named person must argue against the emerging answer
questions.why: Attacks groupthink and confirmation. See §6.4.

questions.stem: Describe 'set criteria first'.
options: Agree how options will be judged before any option exists
questions.why: Attacks confirmation and anchoring; the one to remember. See §6.4.

questions.stem: Describe 'ask for the disconfirming case'.
options: 'What would have to be true for this to be wrong?'
questions.why: Attacks confirmation and overconfidence. See §6.4.

questions.stem: Describe 'ignore what is spent'.
options: Judge only future costs and benefits, from today forward
Keep spending to protect the investment
questions.why: Attacks sunk cost. See §6.4.

questions.stem: Explain why 'be objective' attacks nothing.
options: A general instruction changes no procedure; each method must match a specific bias
questions.why: Match the method to the bias. See §6.4.

questions.stem: Describe a pre-mortem.
options: Assume the plan has already failed and ask why, before you commit
Ask why something failed after it failed
questions.why: The highest-value technique in the chapter. See §6.5.

questions.stem: Identify the four steps of a pre-mortem in order.
options: State the failure as fact; everyone writes alone; read out in rotation without comment; change the plan for the top three
questions.why: Silence first, no discussion until every reason is on the board. See §6.5.

questions.stem: Explain why a pre-mortem works when 'any concerns?' does not.
options: Assuming the failure has already happened removes the social cost of objecting
questions.why: Nobody is being disloyal; everyone is explaining history. See §6.5.

questions.stem: Identify what step 2 of the pre-mortem requires.
options: Five minutes of silent individual writing, no discussion
questions.why: Everyone writes, alone and silently. See §6.5.

questions.stem: Identify the first item on the decision agenda.
options: Agree the criteria and their weights
questions.why: Before anyone sees an option, so it cannot be tuned to a favourite. See §6.6.

questions.stem: Identify the position of the decision itself on the agenda.
options: It is not on the agenda
questions.why: Most meetings begin there and call the rest a formality. See §6.6.

questions.stem: Explain why options are presented without discussion in step 3.
options: It keeps generating separate from judging
questions.why: Generating separate from judging. See §6.6.

questions.stem: Explain why each person writes a private view in step 2.
options: It removes anchoring on whoever speaks first
questions.why: Removes anchoring on the first speaker. See §6.6.

questions.stem: Explain why the challenger is a named role in step 4.
options: It makes objection a role, not an act of disloyalty
questions.why: Objection becomes a role. See §6.6.

questions.stem: Classify 'too much has been invested to stop' from the delivery-app project head.
questions.why: Past spending treated as a reason to keep spending. See §6.1 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Classify the consultant's 400,000-dirham estimate that every later figure orbited.
questions.why: The first number heard drags later estimates. See §6.1.

questions.stem: Classify a satisfaction survey written by the project sponsor.
questions.why: The survey designed to prove the sponsor right. See §6.1.

questions.stem: Classify a board member's memory of a competitor's app failing being treated as proof.
questions.why: What comes to mind easily feels more likely. See §6.1.

questions.stem: Analyse the delivery-app case (400,000 estimate → 1.9 million). Determine the bias that did most damage.
options: Sunk cost — it kept the project alive after the warning in month nine
questions.why: The warning was ignored because of what had been spent. See Exercise 1 and §6.1.

questions.stem: Classify a launch date set again after it has been missed three times.
questions.why: Confidence exceeds accuracy. See §6.1.

questions.stem: Classify a meeting where everyone nods and three people privately disagree.
questions.why: The wish for agreement suppresses objection. See §6.1.

questions.stem: Analyse a manager who says 'I know about anchoring, so I will not anchor'. Determine the chapter's view.
options: Awareness does not protect in the moment — change the process instead
questions.why: People just taught anchoring still anchor. See §6.2.

questions.stem: Analyse the classmate's claim 'if I cannot stop doing it, why learn the names?'. Determine the answer.
options: Names let you diagnose it in others and afterwards in yourself, and design processes against it
questions.why: Recognition plus process design. See §6.2 and Exercise 4.

questions.stem: Determine who has the power to build debiasing into a process.
options: Whoever designs the meeting — and if they are the biased one, the agenda must be agreed before options exist
questions.why: Set the process before the favourite appears. See §6.2, §6.6 and Exercise 4.

questions.stem: Classify a machine failure rate taken from ten years of logs.
questions.why: Known outcomes and odds. See §6.3.

questions.stem: Classify 'how customers will react to a new store format'.
questions.why: Neither odds nor outcomes known. See §6.3.

questions.stem: Analyse the 400,000-dirham app estimate. Determine whether it was a risk judgement or uncertainty dressed as risk.
options: Uncertainty dressed as risk — nobody knew the odds of a custom build
questions.why: A precise number for an unknowable outcome. See Exercise 1 and §6.3.

questions.stem: Classify a five-year sales forecast with two decimal places for a brand-new product.
options: Overconfidence with formatting — uncertainty dressed as risk
questions.why: Not analysis; formatting. See §6.3.

questions.stem: Select the method that attacks sunk cost.
options: Ignore what is spent — judge from today forward
questions.why: Only future costs and benefits. See §6.4.

questions.stem: Select the method that attacks anchoring on whoever speaks first.
questions.why: Private views before discussion. See §6.4.

questions.stem: Select the method the chapter says to remember above all.
options: Set criteria first — free, ten minutes, removes the commonest smuggling of a favourite
questions.why: The one to remember. See §6.4.

questions.stem: Determine the method a manager uses when asking 'what would have to be true for this to be wrong?'.
questions.why: Attacks confirmation and overconfidence. See §6.4.

questions.stem: Analyse a board that tells itself to 'stay objective' before a technology decision. Determine the weakness.
options: A general instruction attacks no specific bias; a procedure must change
questions.why: Match the method to the bias. See §6.4.

questions.stem: Analyse a pre-mortem where the manager asks 'any concerns?' and opens discussion. Determine the broken rule.
options: Silent individual writing first — discussion opened too early
questions.why: Silence first, read out in rotation. See §6.5.

questions.stem: Determine the correct wording to start a pre-mortem.
options: 'It is one year from now. We did this and it failed badly.'
questions.why: State it as fact, not possibility. See §6.5.

questions.stem: Determine what to do with the three most likely failure reasons.
options: Change the plan so each is less likely, or agree how to spot it early
Blame the person who wrote them
questions.why: Step 4 of the pre-mortem. See §6.5.

questions.stem: Analyse why someone 'privately held a reason and did not say it' before a pre-mortem. Determine the social cause.
options: Objecting felt disloyal; the pre-mortem removes that cost
questions.why: The pre-mortem removes the social cost of objecting. See §6.5 and Exercise 3.

questions.stem: Analyse an agenda that starts with 'the CEO presents the preferred option'. Determine the fault.
options: Anchoring on the first speaker and criteria tuned to the favourite — criteria and private views must come first
questions.why: Steps 1 and 2 come before any option. See §6.6.

questions.stem: Determine which agenda step attacks the sponsor's biased survey from the retailer case.
options: Step 1 — criteria agreed before options, so a survey cannot be tuned to prove a favourite
questions.why: Criteria first prevents confirmation. See §6.6 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Select the agenda step to defend hardest if the project head wants it removed.
options: Step 4 — the named challenger, because it is what makes objection safe
questions.why: Objection as a role, not disloyalty. See §6.6 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Determine one measurable sign a year later that the redesigned process worked.
options: Fewer projects whose final cost exceeded the estimate by a large margin
questions.why: Name one thing you could measure. See Exercise 2 and §6.6.

questions.stem: Analyse a meeting that scores options against criteria chosen after seeing the options. Determine the problem.
options: The criteria were tuned to a favourite — confirmation and anchoring
questions.why: Criteria before options. See §6.6 and §6.4.

questions.stem: Determine the right move for 'will staff use the new rota system?'.
options: Test cheaply on one shift, learn, then decide
questions.why: It is uncertainty, not risk. See §6.3.

questions.stem: Analyse a bias that 'helps more often than it harms'. Select the chapter's likely example.
options: Availability — a vivid near-miss makes a real safety risk feel urgent
questions.why: Exercise 4 asks you to defend one with a specific situation. See §6.1 and Exercise 4.

questions.stem: Determine what CLO 2 assesses about bias.
options: Diagnosing bias in a decision by naming it with evidence
questions.why: Recognition is useful for diagnosis. See §6.2.

questions.stem: Determine the chapter's judgement on 'any concerns?' as a way to surface risks.
options: It fails — objecting out loud feels disloyal, so people stay silent
It is step 1 of the agenda
questions.why: Why the pre-mortem works when this does not. See §6.5.
